coach_says: Taking back on d5 with the queen leaves your e6 pawn blocking your c8 bishop, so nothing guards g4, and your dark-squared bishop is already gone. White answers Qg4, hitting g7, and you have to play Kf8 and give up castling. Recapture with the pawn, exd5: it opens the c8 bishop's diagonal so Qg4 just loses the queen to Bxg4, and you can castle next. After a trade of your dark-squared bishop, check what guards g7 before you pull your queen away.

Qb3 puts your queen where Black's pawns can kick it: ...c4 attacks it, and after dxc4 bxc4 (or ...cxd3) it has to go back to d1, so you have just lost time. Black's pawns gain space on the queenside and the d3 square becomes a home for a knight via e5. Your king is still in the centre, so castle first (O-O) and only bring the queen out where pawns can't chase it with gain of time.

Bg4 attacks the queen, but it simply moves to b3, a better square with gain of time. Your f-pawn is gone, so the queen and the c4 bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal stop you castling (g8 is covered) and threaten Bf7+ and Bxg6. The bishop has also left b7 without a defender. Then f3 kicks your bishop away again. Keep that bishop home guarding your light squares and develop with Nc6, hitting d4 and getting ready for ...e5.
also: attacking the queen just helps it

coach_says: Black's last move, Bd7, attacked your a4 pawn, and nothing defends it. Ng4 ignores that, so Black takes Bxa4 for free. Worse, your king is castled on the queenside, so Black's a-pawn and b-pawn then run at it. Before starting your own play, ask what your opponent's last move threatens: b3 defends a4 and keeps the pawn shield in front of your king closed.
also: pawn shield in front of castled king
